Woolmark logo

The International Wool Secretariat’s Woolmark of 1964: a skein of wool drawn as three looped bands of black and white stripes.

Source
AGI: Woolmark, 1964
Creator
Franco Grignani (entered as “Francesco Seraglio” or “Saroglia”)
Made
1963 (competition); launched 1964
Style
Op art (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
High-contrast, rhythmic, iconic
Evidence
Downloaded and inspected the AGI reproduction of the mark (1600 × 1457 px) in a scratchpad. No image is stored.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Woolmark says that the International Wool Secretariat announced a design competition in 1963, and that the winning design, “a stylised skein of wool”, was “the work of a Milanese designer named Francesco Saroglia”. Woolmark.

AGI attributes the mark to Franco Grignani: he sat on the jury, entered under the alias Francesco Seraglio, and won. AGI. AIGA Eye on Design says the mark was claimed by Grignani in 1975. AIGA Eye on Design.

The V&A’s Riley records instead say that Bridget Riley designed the Woolmark logo. No other source checked here supports that. V&A.

Observed

  • Three looped bands interlace to form a rounded triangle with a small open triangle at the centre.
  • Each band is made of five or six parallel black stripes separated by white gaps. The stripes taper to points at their ends.
  • The stripes thicken on the outer curve and thin on the inner curve, so each loop seems to twist.
  • The mark is pure black on white, with no outline or tone.

Why it belongs

The Woolmark carries Grignani’s optical research into a trademark: tapering parallel lines make the flat mark read as a turning, three-dimensional skein.

It shows how op line work can survive at small sizes when the stripes are few and heavy.

Borrow

Draw a mark from a few parallel stripes that taper to points, so that it seems to twist.

Keep op motifs for icons to five or six heavy stripes; fine lines break up at small sizes.
